Yogakuṇḍalī Upaniṣad.
"May He protect us both"—thus the Peace.
Chapter One.
There are three means for conquering the vital winds and two causes of the mind: latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the breath (*samīraṇa*).
When one of these two is destroyed, both of them perish. (1)
Of these two, a person should always first achieve mastery over the breath (samīra);
then, moderate diet, [proper] posture, and thirdly, the movement of power (śakticāla). || 2 ||
I contemplate the reality of the non-dual Brahman as being nothing but my own self, according to the commentary on the *Yogakuṇḍalī Upaniṣad* and the heart-seats of the perfected yogis.

Herein indeed, this *Yogakuṇḍalī Upaniṣad*, which is a branch of the *Kṛṣṇayajurveda*, stands preeminent, being intent upon revealing the yoga of *haṭha* and *lambikā*, and culminating in the non-dual Brahman alone. A brief commentary on it is now commenced.

At the outset, he introduces Haṭhayoga by way of an intermediate statement beginning with "the two causes" (*hetudvayam*). Through the restraint of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the movement and non-movement of the mind (*citta*) occur.
The meaning is that even upon the restraint of either one of these, both are indeed restrained. As a means to that [restraint],...
"Moderate in food," and so forth. || 2 ||
(308) Regarding moderate diet, I shall describe their characteristics; listen with respect, O Gautama:
one's food should be very smooth and sweet, leaving a fourth part of the stomach empty. || 3 ||
That which is consumed for the sake of pleasing Śiva is called "moderate food" (mitāhāra).
Regarding that, [it is said] "very unctuous" (susnigdha) and so forth. 3–4.
Regarding the posture, it is said to be of two kinds: the lotus posture (padmāsana) and likewise the vajra posture (vajrāsana). || 4 ||
If one places both soles of the feet upon the thighs in such a way that they are positioned above them, this shall be the lotus posture (padmāsana), which destroys all sins. || 5 ||
One should place the root of the left foot below the *kanda* (the bulbous root) and the other [foot] above it;
with the neck, head, and body held erect, this is called the *vajrāsana* (diamond posture).
In that regard, the definition of the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) is as follows: "of the two thighs," etc. (5–6).
The activation of the power (śakti) and its two means are indeed the Kuṇḍalinī herself; the wise man should activate that power.
The movement of the power from its own place up to the middle of the eyebrows is called "the activation of the power" (śakticālana). || 7 ||
In accomplishing that, two things are primary: the movement of Sarasvatī and the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa). Furthermore, through practice, Kuṇḍalinī becomes straightened.

(309) To the question "What is that activation of power? [the answer is] "The Kuṇḍalī itself" (verse 7). To the question "What is its means of accomplishment? [the answer is] "In the means of accomplishing it" (verses 8–14).
The Shaking of Sarasvatī:
First, I shall describe to you the shaking of Sarasvatī.
Sarasvatī was described by the knowers of antiquity as being identical with Arundhatī. (9)
By the movement of which the Kuṇḍalinī does not move by itself—
[this is achieved] when the prāṇa flows through the Iḍā, having firmly assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana).
Then the wise one, having spread out a cloth twelve finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths in width, should wrap that tube with it.
One should hold [the vessel] firmly with both hands using the thumbs and index fingers;
one should move it back and forth according to one's strength, from left to right and again from right to left.
For a period of two muhūrtas, the wise practitioner should move [the breath] fearlessly;
he should draw it slightly upward toward the Suṣumnā, which has entered Kuṇḍalinī.
By that [means], Kuṇḍalinī shall go to the mouth of that Suṣumnā;
therefore, this Prāṇa abandons [its usual path] and goes spontaneously into the Suṣumnā. || 14 ||
One should provide relief for the abdomen once the constriction of the throat has been effected;
by the movement of Sarasvatī, the vital air (marut) in the chest shall rise upward.
One should expel the breath through the Sūrya [nāḍī] during the movement of Sarasvatī;
having constricted the throat, the wind (marut) in the chest shall move upward.
Therefore, one should constantly cause Sarasvatī, who contains sound within her, to flow;
by the mere flowing of her, the yogi is liberated from diseases. (17)
Gulma, ascites, splenic disorders, and whatever other ailments reside within the abdomen—all these diseases are certainly destroyed by the movement of the Śakti. || 18 ||

Preceded by the three bindings starting from the *mūlādhāra*, through the movement of Sarasvatī, the wind (vital air) shall rise upward from the chest. This has already been explained. Because it is so, therefore—[the various types of] breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Now I shall briefly explain the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇarodha).
The vital breath is the wind residing within the body; its retention is known as āyāma or kumbhaka. || 19 ||
That very [practice] is said to be of two kinds: the combined (sahita) and likewise the solitary (kevala).
One should practice the combined method as long as the accomplishment of the solitary method has not been attained.
Sūryabheda, ujjāyī, śītalī, and the fourth, bhastrī—
along with these very varieties, the kumbha [breath-retention] which occurs is the sahita-kumbhaka.
The solar kumbhaka should be performed in a pure, secluded place, free from gravel and the like,
extending for a distance of one bow-length, and devoid of cold, fire, and water. || 22 ||
On a pure seat that is neither too high nor too low, which is comfortable and pleasant,
one should assume the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) and perform the movement of Sarasvatī.
Having slowly drawn in the external air through the right channel (dakṣanāḍī), one should fill the breath as desired and then exhale it through the left channel (iḍā). || 24 ||
Or, during the purification of the skull (kapāla), one should slowly exhale the breath;
this destroys the fourfold defects of wind (vāta) as well as the defects of worms (kṛmi).
This task, known as the piercing of the sun (*sūryabheda*), is to be performed again and again;
it consists of four parts and is of four kinds. (25–42)
Ujjāyī kumbhaka:
having restrained the mouth, one slowly draws in the breath through both nostrils. (26)
Just as it reaches resonantly from the throat down to the heart, one should retain the breath as before and then exhale through the iḍā. || 27 ||
It removes the fire arising from the head, it is supreme in removing phlegm from the throat, it is meritorious, it removes all diseases, and it increases the digestive fire of the body. (28)
The kumbhaka known as ujjāyī should be performed while walking or standing; it cures intestinal dropsy and destroys the defects residing within the bodily constituents (dhātus).
In the *śītalī-kumbhaka*, the wise practitioner, having drawn in the air with the tongue as before during the retention (*kumbhaka*),
should slowly exhale the breath through both nostrils. (30)
This kumbhaka, named Śītalī, destroys disorders such as abdominal tumors and splenic enlargement, as well as wasting, bile, fever, thirst, and poisons. (31)
Then, having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), with neck and abdomen held straight, the wise practitioner,
having carefully restrained the mouth, should exhale the breath through the nose by means of the bellows-retention (bhastrākumbhaka).
Just as it strikes from the throat onto the skull with a sound,
one should then forcefully fill the breath slightly as far as the heart-lotus.
One should cause it to be purged again in that same manner and fill it again and again,
just as the bellows of smiths are moved by the force of the wind.
In that very same manner, one should slowly move the breath situated within one's own body; then, one should exhale through the right nostril (sūryanāḍī) until fatigue arises in the body. || 35 ||
Just as the abdomen becomes full, it likewise becomes light when one firmly holds the middle of the nose with the two index fingers, excluding the thumbs. 36.
Having performed the kumbhaka as before, one should exhale the breath through the iḍā;
this destroys the fire arising in the throat and increases the digestive fire of the body. (37)

This meritorious [teaching] awakens the Kuṇḍalinī; it destroys sin, bestows auspiciousness and happiness, and removes the obstructions such as phlegm located within the opening of the Brahma-nāḍī. (38)
This kumbhaka known as *bhastrā* must specifically be performed to pierce the three knots produced by the three *guṇas*. (39)
The Procedure for the Three Locks:
When the kumbhaka of all four types has arrived, these three locks (bandhas) should be performed by yogis who are free from impurity. (40)
The first is the root-bind (mūlabandha), the second is named the upward-flight (uḍḍīyaṇa), and the third is the throat-hold (jālandhara); their characteristics are now described. (41)
The *mūlabandha* forcibly causes the downward-moving *apāna* wind to move upward;
by means of this contraction, it is called *mūlabandha*. (42)
When the apāna moves upward and reaches the circle of fire,
then a long flame of fire increases, driven by the wind.
Then the fire and the downward-breath (apāna) went toward the vital breath (prāṇa), whose nature is heat;
by that [heat] being utterly inflamed, the fire born of the body likewise blazed up.
By that [means], the sleeping Kuṇḍalinī, being thoroughly heated, becomes fully awakened;
like a female serpent struck by a staff, she hisses and attains straightness. (45)
Since one enters the interior of the Brahma-nāḍī by means of entering the *bila*, therefore the *mūlabandha* should always be performed by yogis at all times. (46)
Slain and shaken. || 43-62 ||

The Uḍḍiyāṇa-bandha should be performed at the end of the retention (kumbhaka) and at the beginning of the exhalation (recaka); it is called Uḍḍiyāṇa because by means of this binding, the vital breath (prāṇa) is made to soar up into the Suṣumnā. || 47 ||
Therefore, this is proclaimed by yogis as the Uḍḍīyāna [bandha].
When in the vajrāsana posture, one should firmly hold the feet with both hands. (48)
And near the region of the ankles, one should press upon the *kanda*;
one should maintain a backward contraction in the abdomen, at the heart, and in the throat. (49)
When the breath gradually reaches the junction of the navel, one should constantly and slowly expel the impurities of the abdomen. (50)

The Jālandhara-bandha should be performed at the end of the inhalation (pūraka); this bandha, named Jālandhara, consists of the contraction of the throat and serves to block the passage of the vital air. || 51 ||
When the throat is quickly constricted by contracting the lower part, and the middle [part] is drawn back, the vital breath (prāṇa) shall enter the Brahma-nāḍī. || 52 ||
Having properly assumed the posture in the very sequence previously described,
and having performed the movement of Sarasvatī, one should restrain the vital breath (prāṇa).
Regarding the rule for the number of practice-retentions (abhyāsakumbhaka):
on the first day, four retentions should be performed, each numbering ten; likewise, on the second day, five [retentions] should be performed.
On the third day, twenty [breaths] are sufficient; then, one should daily perform the *kumbhaka* for twenty-one days, increasing by five each day, always accompanied by the three *bandhas*.

Obstacles to the practice of yoga and their abandonment: sleeping by day and staying awake at night; excessive sexual intercourse; constant frequenting of many places; and the suppression of urine and feces. (56)

Furthermore, diseases arise quickly from the faults of an uneven posture and from the exertion of mental concentration on the vital breath; however, if the practitioner of restraint stabilizes [the mind], he shall suppress them. (57)
It is said that "a disease has arisen in me due to the practice of yoga";
therefore, one should abandon the practice—this is called the first obstacle. (58)
The second is called doubt, the third is negligence;
the fourth is called laziness, and the fifth is in the form of sleep. (59)
The sixth is detachment, the seventh is proclaimed to be delusion,
the eighth is the object itself, and the ninth is remembered as the "Inexpressible" (anākhyam).
The failure to attain the reality of yoga is declared by the wise to be the tenth [obstacle].
Thus, the wise man should abandon these ten obstacles through discernment. 61.
Through the practice of yoga, the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī occurs;
thereafter, the practice of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) should be performed constantly with a mind established in pure being (sattva).
Then the mind dissolves into the Suṣumnā, and the vital air no longer wanders astray.
When the impurity has been dried up, the yogi’s movement is then set in motion;
he forcibly causes the downward-moving apāna to move upward.
By means of contraction, they call this the "root-lock" (mūlabandha);
the apāna wind, having moved upward, proceeds together with the fire.
Then the fire at the seat of the vital breath, together with the prāṇa and apāna, quickly joins and enters Kuṇḍalī, who lies asleep in a coiled form.
Heated by that fire and impelled by the wind itself, she extends her own body into the interior of the opening of the *suṣumnā*. (66)

Thus, for one who performs *prāṇāyāma* with firm resolve toward sentient beings, the mind and other faculties do not waver, nor does the vital air ever rush about. When the impurities within the channels have been dried up by means of pure *kumbhaka*,
and the movement of the vital air (*prāṇa*) in the *suṣumnā* has been set in motion and then restrained— if that occurs, then this yogi [attains success].
The meaning is "it may be. || 63-64 || It goes; it has gone. || 65 || Kuṇḍalinī has been moved. || 66-67 ||
By piercing the three knots, the Kuṇḍalinī proceeds to the Sahasrāra;
then, having burst through the Brahma-knot arising from the quality of Rajas, she flashes swiftly at the mouth of the Suṣumnā like a streak of lightning. (67)
Established in the heart, it quickly ascends to the Viṣṇugranthi;
and that which exists above it proceeds upward to the Rudragranthi arising therefrom. (68)
Having pierced through the middle of the eyebrows, it goes to the orb of the cool-rayed moon,
which is the wheel known as Anāhata, endowed with sixteen petals.
There, the sun, by its planetary power, dries up the liquid produced from the cool-rayed moon when it is moved by the force of the vital breath (prāṇa). 70.
How can that which is hot, when sprinkled there where the lunar wheel resides—which consists of pure, fluid phlegm—swallow it, given that [the latter] is cold by nature? || 71 ||
In that very same way, the white lunar form indeed heats with impetuosity;
agitated, it flows upward, and at that moment it streams forth even more intensely.
Because of the power of relishing that [bliss], the mind of one who is established in the Self and delights in the Self becomes directed toward external objects;
yet, having experienced that very [state] as supreme, the youth remains healthy and self-rejoicing. (73)

That which arises from it is the Rudra-granthi, arising from the base of the Ājñā-cakra. It is endowed with sixteen petals—eight primary petals and likewise eight secondary petals, totaling sixteen. When the vital breath dries up the fluid born of the moon in the heart...

Then, when the blood and other elements there are set in motion by the force of the *prāṇa*, the Sun shall swallow—that is, dry up—the blood, bile, and so forth from the *graha*. [70] Thereafter, "the lunar wheel has gone into the *prāṇa*. [71]
It flows exceedingly—that is to say, it is a stream of nectar (amṛtadhārā).

By virtue of tasting this stream of nectar, the mind becomes indifferent toward and withdrawn from uneven objects; one who possesses such a mind is a sage (muni) delighting in the Self (ātmarata), and that very state is the supreme [bliss] called nectar.

"Having consumed the oblation, one should be established in oneself; being established in oneself, one delights in the Self"—in this [verse], there is the elision of the visarga, the letter *t*, and the vowel *a*. || 73 ||

The dissolution of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, as well as the outward expansion of those dissolved [energies], occurs; and Kuṇḍalinī goes to the station consisting of the eightfold Prakṛti.
Embracing Śiva, she proceeds; embracing him, she dissolves.
Thus, after that, within the white dust of the upper and lower Śivās,
the vital air (māruta) moves equally as both prāṇa and apāna, born together in that very same manner.
Even when the object is small and the mind is small, the expressive word expands excessively;
it drives forth all the vital winds like gold in a furnace heated by fire.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "The material nature," and so forth:
"Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and likewise ego—this material nature of mine is divided eightfold."

Thus, in accordance with the *Smṛti*, having abandoned the form of the eightfold group of one's own innate nature (*svāttaprakṛtyaṣṭaka*), and having embraced the eye, mind, vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so forth, when the *Kuṇḍalinī*— having embraced everything— dissolves into the *sahasrāra*, then [she dissolves] into Śiva, who is the white *rajas* above; thus it is said in the passage beginning "in the white *rajas* above."
Then, following the dissolution of Kuṇḍalinī, in the subsequent moment, the solar *jīvatattva* (the individual soul-principle) and its *rajas*,

as well as the lunar *aiśvara* (divine) *śukla* and its *rajas-śukla*, dissolve into Śiva, the Supreme Self, who is adorned with the thousand-petalled lotus (*sahasrāra*) and who devours all that is inauspicious apart from Himself. Thereafter, in the moment following that—

Even the vital air (māruta) dissolves. Regarding how the innate breath and so forth dissolve: just as day and night become equal at the two innate junctions (saṃdhyā), in the very same way, the innate pair—the prāṇa and apāna—become equal within the innate state characterized by abiding in the nature of the fourth (turya), which is the non-conceptual state.

The meaning is that this very state—where the upward and downward movements have become sparse and one has attained a state of non-activity—is the dissolution of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the rest. When the vital breath, mind, speech, and so forth have thus dissolved, how can they spread internally or externally? In this regard, as for the external, even something extremely small, such as a jar, exists only as something distinct from oneself; therefore, it is called "insignificant" (*bhūtamalpa*).

When that subtle [subtle element] is remembered, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) flows forth. When one thinks that there exists something small or slight apart from oneself—that "small mind" (*manolpa*)—then, upon the conceptualization of that "small mind," the mind, consisting of volition and doubt, flows forth. But when the designator (the word) is remembered as being distinct from oneself, then...

The activity of speech proceeds; thus, having arisen, the vital breath, mind, speech, and so forth, increase. When the completion of the vital breath and the other [faculties] has occurred, all the winds such as the vital breath pervade from head to foot, like molten gold poured into a mold.
"He causes to flow" (dhāvayati) means "they flow," in the sense that they exist pervading [the body] from head to foot. || 76 ||

Through the experience of everything as pure consciousness within samādhi, the physical body is transformed into a divine form; the body becomes exceedingly pure and attains the state of being a subtle, transportable vehicle (ativāhika).
Free from the state of insentience, stainless, and consisting of pure consciousness—this is its primary subtle body (ativāhika), which belongs to all beings and is identical with me. (78)
"Liberation from birth and existence is the delusion of that which has the form of Time"—thus the intellect, being its own true nature, [perceives it] like a snake in a rope. (79)
Everything arises as mere falsehood and dissolves as mere falsehood,
just as the notion of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell arises for a man and a woman who are deluded.

The identity of the individual body and the cosmic egg, as well as that of the subtle body (liṅga) and the thread-like vital force (sūtra), the identity of deep sleep and the undifferentiated state, and the identity of the self-luminous conscious Self—[all these are realized]. 81.

Furthermore, he says "ādhibhautika" etc., to show that in the state of meditative absorption (*samāhitāvasthā*), all this culminates in pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) alone. Regarding the physical body imagined by one's own ignorance (*svājñavikalpita*), it exists as the "ādhibhautikadeha"; and that very physical body is the Self, the inward-facing reality (*pratyak*).

That which exists with reference to the deity is the *ādhidaivika* (divine) body; one should dissolve that *ādhidaivika* body—which is non-different from the innermost Self (*pratyag-abhinna-paramātman*)—into its true nature as that alone. Thereafter, having abandoned the state of regarding the previously occupied body as a mere physical vessel like a garment soiled with dirt, [one remains as the Self].

The meaning is that one attains the very state of pure Brahman; by being the support for the phenomenal world imagined through one's own ignorance, it carries [the self] everywhere, and thus one reaches the state of Brahman, which is the state of the subtle body (*ātivāhikatā*). Whatever inert body and so forth, distinct from oneself, has been experienced—all that— || 77 || [is sublated].

That which is free from the state of insentience, stainless, and consisting of pure consciousness; that which is my own self (*madātmaka*), the substratum for the superimposition and negation of all things such as the body and so forth that are to be presided over;

that Brahman which is non-different from the inner self (*pratyagabhinna*) that serves as the objective support for the notion of "I" (*asmat-pratyaya-ālambana-bhūta*)—its nature is indeed that of a subtle, transportive vehicle (*ativāhikatva*).

"Principal" means "real. (78) If, for you, a cognition of attributes arises regarding Brahman—which is non-different from the inner self (pratyak) that transcends the external (parāk)—then, having arisen, it "becomes"; thus, the state of being its "wife" is the manifestation of its possessing attributes. The establishment of its negation is liberation from that. Thus...
The meaning is this: even the statement that negates [everything] along with its distinctions is merely an error of knowledge regarding Brahman in the form of time;

since Brahman alone—established by the negation of all—is without a counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogika*), the statement that negates the error of "there is" or "there is not" anything other than itself is itself worthy of being negated.

Thus, having realized that which remains as one's own residual state through the cognition of that very residue, the abiding in one's own true nature simultaneously with that realization is itself liberation. || 79 ||
Beyond that, during the state of one's own ignorance, whatever is experienced— like a snake in a rope,
or like the perception of "this is silver" arising from a mistaken delusion in a mother-of-pearl shell for a man and woman— it all arises as mere falsehood and dissolves as mere falsehood.

In reality, whether the delusion of the vision of one's own ignorance and so forth exists or not, Brahman alone remains as that which is without a counterpart; this is the established conclusion. How, then, is it said that "Brahman alone remains"?
If you consider the distinction between the individual (vyaṣṭi) and the collective (samaṣṭi),

then [you must acknowledge] the differentiation beginning with Viśva and ending with Turiya, which consists of the manifold (prapañca) of the individual and the collective, along with their superimposition (āropa) and negation (apavāda), and their substratum (ādhāra).
One should contemplate the identity [of the self] with everything from Virāj up to Turya; thus he says: "The body," etc.
The term "identity" is intended to indicate the identity of Viśva and Virāj.
When the qualified nature residing in that identity—which presupposes difference—has ceased, [one reaches] Brahman.
The meaning is that only one's own nature, free from all counterparts, remains. || 81 ||
The power of the yoga of samādhi is the auspicious one named Kuṇḍalinī, resembling a lotus fiber;
she [coils] around the root-knoll with the tip of her hood, like a lotus bulb.
Grasping the tail with the mouth and joined at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
the practitioner, seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana) and composed, should contract the anus.
Making the wind move upward with a mind fixed in *kumbhaka*, the fire situated in the *svādhiṣṭhāna* blazes by the force of the impact of the wind. (84)
Awakened by the impact of the fire and the impact of the wind,
the king of serpents then pierces the Brahma-knot and thereafter pierces the Viṣṇu-knot.
Having pierced the Rudra-knot, she indeed splits the six lotuses;
in the thousand-petaled lotus, the Śakti rejoices together with Śiva. (86)
That very state is to be known as supreme; that alone is the cause of liberation.
Thus, as a means for attaining such knowledge, he explains the yoga of samādhi: "Power," and so forth.
82–84 || Regarding the word "ghātena" here, the form "ghātoḥ" is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage. || 85 ||

Immediately after piercing the three knots that adorn the six cakras, this Kuṇḍalinī-śakti rejoices with Śiva in the thousand-petalled lotus (sahasrāra). Having swallowed the manifold world of duality imagined by herself and having attained the form of the non-dual knowledge of Brahman, she herself also—

That state which has been described as culminating in Brahman alone, which is without any counterpart, should be known as the supreme disembodied liberation (videhamukti). That very state is the cause of bliss, because it is the means for the manifestation of supreme bliss. The word "iti" signifies the conclusion of Haṭhayoga.
And [the word "iti"] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the chapter. || 87 ||
Thus ends the first chapter.
The second chapter:
The Science of Khecarī.
Now I shall fully proclaim the lore known as Khecarī, by which one becomes free from old age and death in this world, having attained such realization.
O Sage, having seen this knowledge, one who is seized by death, disease, and old age should firm up their resolve and practice the Khecarī [vidyā].
On this earth, he who knows the Khecarī [mudrā]—which destroys old age, death, and disease—both in its literal text and its meaning, through the practice and application thereof, [is liberated]. (3)
O Sage, one should take refuge in him, regarding him as a guru with one's whole being;
for the Khecarī-vidyā is difficult to attain, and its practice is likewise difficult to achieve.
Practice and union do not succeed simultaneously;
those devoted solely to practice do not find union.
O Brahmin, one may occasionally attain practice in one birth after another;
yet that meeting with [the right] births is not obtained even at the end of a hundred lifetimes.
Having practiced for the end of many births and perfected that state of being,
some yogi attains union (melana) somewhere in another birth.
But when the yogin obtains the union from the mouth of the Guru,
then he attains that perfection which has been described in the lineage of the scriptures.
When one attains a union both in terms of the text and its meaning,
then one attains the state of Śiva, liberated from all worldly existence.
Even teachers would not be able to fully understand it without the scripture;
therefore, O Sage, this scripture is most difficult to obtain, yet it has been acquired. (10)
As long as the scripture is not obtained, the ascetic should wander the earth;
when the scripture is obtained, then success rests in the palm of one's hand.
Success is not seen in the three worlds without the scripture;
therefore, one should honor the giver of the scripture, the infallible bestower of the *melana*. (12)
One should take refuge in Śiva, considering him the bestower of that practice;
having received this scripture from me, one should not reveal it to others. (13)
Therefore, O Brahmin, one who understands this should protect [the secret] with every effort wherever the Guru resides, the bestower of divine yoga. (14)
Having gone there and received the *khecarī* vidyā taught by him, he was told:
"First, you should practice it correctly and without sloth. (15)
By means of this vidyā, the yogi shall become a possessor of the siddhi of Khecarī;
by uniting Khecarī with Khecarī through the filling of the seed-syllable of Khecarī.
Having become the sovereign of the sky-dwellers (*khecaras*), one shall dwell eternally among the sky-dwellers.
Having expounded the entire essence of *haṭhayoga* together with knowledge, he explains the *lambikā-yoga* in detail, beginning with "Now" (*atha*). Just as it is, exactly as it is... to me.
From me [it is said]: || 13-15 || By filling [the channels] with the seed-syllable of the Khecarī, beginning with *hrīṃ*, the yogi—
whose mind and breath have dissolved into the internal object of focus— always abides with a gaze of fixed pupils, looking outward below yet not seeing anything.
Indeed, that mudrā becomes Khecarī when it is one-pointedly focused on the objective; auspicious and devoid of both the void and the non-void, she flashes forth as the reality and the state of Viṣṇu.
Thus, he who passes his time practicing the yoga of Khecarī by means of the Khecarīmudrā established in the Śrutis. || 16 ||
At the end of his body, that yogi becomes the sun, the sovereign of the sky-farers, and shall dwell eternally among the sky-farers in the worlds accessible to those who travel through the sky.
p. 324) The extraction of the King of Mantras of Khecarī:
[the syllable] KHE, which is the abode of the sky-farers (khecaras), adorned with the fire and water mandalas. || 17 ||
The seed-syllable of the Khecarī has been declared; by means of it, Yoga is accomplished.
One should extract the ninth part of the lunar digits as the phoneme in reverse order. (18)
Therefore, O Sage, the syllable consisting of three parts is said to have the form of the moon;
from that [syllable], the eighth letter in reverse order is another.
Know that likewise, that [syllable] is supreme; the fifth [vowel] is also its beginning.
And when it is joined with the Moon (the letter *i*) in various ways, this is proclaimed as the *kūṭa*. || 20 ||

He extracts the King of Melana Mantras: "Khecara," etc. That which moves by virtue of denoting the sky (*kha*) is *khecara*, the letter *ha*. "Abode" (*āvasatha*) is the power of retention (*dhāraṇā*), the letter *ī*. "Fire" (*ra*) is the letter *ra*.
"The water-mandala" is the *bindu*. All of this combined and adorned results in *hrīṃ*. || 17 ||
The seed-syllable of Khecarī is thus declared; by that alone, the yoga of the uvula (lambikā) is accomplished.

It should be known that the remaining six seed-syllables are also adorned by the sphere of water (the letter *va*). The lunar portion is the letter *sa*; that is the seed-syllable of the Moon. By reversing that, one should extract its ninth phoneme, which is *bha*. || 18 ||

Therefore, from the letter *bha*, moving in direct order (*anuloma*), the third part is declared to be the seed-syllable of the Moon, namely *sa*. From that letter *sa*, moving in reverse order (*viloma*), one should extract the other eighth syllable, namely *ma*.
Likewise, from the letter *ma*, moving in reverse order, know the other fifth syllable to be *pa*. Furthermore, of the Moon...

One should extract the seed-syllable *sam*. Joined with many *ka*s, *ṣa*s, and *bindu*s, this *kūṭa* is *kṣam*. In total, there are seven seed-syllables: *hrīṃ*, *bhaṃ*, *saṃ*, *maṃ*, *paṃ*, *saṃ*, and *kṣaṃ*. (20–21)
Through the recitation of mantras, the siddhi of Khecarī is attained;
it is to be obtained through the instruction of the Guru and bestows success in all yogas.
For that [yogi], the illusion born of the body, which resides in the restrained senses, [is overcome].
Even in a dream, one shall never fail to obtain [the fruit] from constantly reciting this twelve times; indeed, even one who is well-restrained should recite this five hundred thousand times. (22)
For him, the siddhi of the Śrīkhecarī [mudrā] proceeds spontaneously;
all obstacles perish and the deities become propitious. (23)
There will be the destruction of wrinkles and grey hair; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus obtained the Mahāvidyā, one should then perform its practice.
Otherwise, O Brahmā, one suffers; there is no success on the path of the Khecarī, for he who does not obtain the nectar-like Vidyā during the practice of its rules.
Therefore, having obtained the vidyā at the time of initiation and other such occasions, one should always recite it;
otherwise, O Brahmin, being deprived of it, one shall not attain any accomplishment whatsoever.
When this scripture is obtained, then one should take recourse in the knowledge;
thereupon, the sage quickly attains that perfection which has been proclaimed therein. || 27 ||
The meaning is that he who recites this twelve times daily constantly transcends illusion.
(22) The sequence for practicing Khecarī: having drawn up the root of the palate for seven days, the knower of the Self—
One should completely purify all impurity according to the method taught by one's own guru. || 28 ||
Then, having taken up a very sharp, smooth, and stainless blade resembling the leaf of the *snuhī* plant, one should cut off [the hair] only to the extent of a single hair's breadth.
Having discarded [the previous treatment], one should draw it out with powdered rock salt (*saindhava*) and *pathyā*;
when seven days have passed again, one should shave it down to the length of a hair.
In this manner, one should practice with constant diligence for six months;
after six months, the binding of the vessels at the root of the tongue is destroyed.
Then, the yogi who knows the rules for the timing of the practice should wrap the head— the abode of Vāgīśvarī— with a cloth and slowly draw it upward.
Furthermore, O Sage, by constant friction for just six months,
it reaches as far as the middle of the eyebrows and transversely to the openings of the ears.
Then, through its gradual movement, it reaches the root of the chin;
again, after three years, it proceeds effortlessly.
O Sage, it ascends vertically to the hairline and extends laterally to the limits of the shoulders;
then, after another three years, it reaches down as far as the pit of the throat.
It remains covering the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), there is no doubt;
it extends horizontally to the surface of the crown of the head and downwards as far as the cavity of the throat. || 36 ||
Gradually, having burst open the great adamantine door-panel from the head,
the previously mentioned mantra joined with the seed-syllable indeed attains that which is difficult to obtain.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with that [mantra] differentiated by the six vowels;
one should thus perform the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) for the sake of attaining all perfections and other goals.
One should practice in this manner very gradually, and certainly not all at once; for if one attempts it all at once, the body will meet with destruction. (39)
Therefore, O bull among sages, one should practice this gradually and slowly;
and when the tongue reaches the aperture of Brahmā via the external path, [success is attained]. (40)
Then, O Brahmin, having rubbed with the tip of his finger that bolt of Brahmā which is difficult to break even for the gods, he should place it upon the tip of his tongue. || 41 ||
Having practiced in this manner for three years, one enters the door of Brahman;
once the door of Brahman has been entered, one should perform the churning correctly.
Some wise ones accomplish [the goal] without churning;
for one who has attained mastery over the *khecarī* mantra, the [result] is accomplished without churning. (43)
By performing both the recitation (japa) and the churning (mathana), one shall quickly obtain the fruit;
[using] a small rod made of gold, silver, or even iron. || 44 ||
Having closed the nostrils with a thread moistened with milk, and having restrained the vital breaths in the heart, one should assume a comfortable posture for oneself. (45)
One should perform gentle churning while fixing the gaze between the eyebrows;
through the very state of this churning for six months, [the goal] is produced.
Just as deep sleep is for children, so should one’s state of being be;
constant churning is not recommended; one should practice it month by month.
The yogi should never allow his tongue to wander from the path;
in this way, at the end of twelve years, perfect accomplishment becomes certain. 48.
One perceives the entire universe within the body due to its non-difference from the Self.
This cosmic egg is the great path, the royal tooth, the upward-moving Kuṇḍalinī. (49)
Thus [it is said].

He describes the sequence of practice: "The palate," etc. (vv. 28–29). "Having abandoned other activities" means that *harītakī* is the meaning of the word *pathyā*. (vv. 30–31). "The head of the abode of Vāgīśvarī" refers to the tip of the tongue.
32–34 || The limit of the horizontal branches means the root of the crest (śikhā). 35–36 ||

The rare [state] is its extreme rarity. (37) By means of the six vowels differentiated [by the nasal sounds], that is to say, by *hrāṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and so forth. (38–40) *Brahmārgala* is the cavity within the tongue. (41–47) Thus, having practiced the *lambikā-vidyā* from the mouth of the Guru for twelve years of observance, [one attains the goal].

The perfection of the *lambikā*-yoga is attained. By the statement "one perceives the entire universe within the body," one sequentially realizes the forms of the Virāṭ, Sūtra, Bīja, and Turya. Wherein the tongue, as the *kuṇḍalinī* above the *rājadanta*, extends into the thousand-petalled lotus (*sahasrāra*), that path is like the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
It occurs because of its excellent path. The word "iti" signifies the conclusion of the yoga of the uvula (lambikā) and also marks the conclusion of the second chapter. || 49 ||
Thus ends the second chapter.
The third chapter: The Mantra of Conjunction.
*Hrīṃ bhaṃ saṃ maṃ paṃ saṃ kṣam*. He recites the *melanamantra* from the throat: *hrīṃ*, etc. (p.
329). There is a distinction in vision based on the divisions of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), the first lunar day (*pratipat*), and the full moon (*pūrṇimā*).
Padmaja said:
O Śaṅkara, regarding the new moon day (amāvāsyā), the first lunar day (pratipad), and the full moon day (paurṇamāsī)—what is their descriptive designation? Tell me this according to the truth.
[Śiva said:

"On the first day of the lunar fortnight, at the improper time, as well as on the new moon (amāvāsyā) and the full moon (paurṇamāsī), one should stabilize it; for that is the path, and not otherwise."

It is said that Brahmā, desiring to know the true nature of the three views and their respective objects, questioned Śiva; thus [the author] says: "The Lotus-born One" (padmaja). The Lord spoke the answer to the question:
"At every step" (pratipad), which refers to the means for perceiving the external, internal, and intermediate objects of focus.
Vision conjoined with the mind is divided into three types according to the distinctions of *amā* and so forth.
Among these, vision with the eyes tightly closed is *amā*; vision with the eyes half-open is *pratipat*;
and vision with the eyes fully open is *pūrṇimā*. In the perception of the target, it is the *pūrṇimā* vision.

It is praised [as follows]: if eye fatigue occurs during the time of practice, then one should look at the new moon (pratipad) out of its proper time, or by means of the full moon (amā). When one has overcome fatigue, then one should stabilize the vision of the full moon itself.
One should observe [the breath] without obstacles, sometimes by the sight of the full moon, sometimes by the sight of the first day of the lunar fortnight, and sometimes by the sight of the new moon.

Thus, because of the statement regarding the Brahman-Pranava, the meaning is that this very path is superior to [the practice of] breath control (prāṇāyāma) involving inhalation (prāṇa) and exhalation (apāna). || 2 ||
The procedure for the vision of the Full Moon:
one who desires sense-objects, being deluded by desire regarding those objects, should always abandon these two alone and take refuge in the Stainless One (Nirañjana). (3)
Furthermore, one who desires his own welfare should renounce everything else;
having placed the mind in the midst of *śakti*, and the *śakti* in the midst of the mind. (4)
Having perceived the mind with the mind, one should abandon it; that is the supreme state.
For the mind alone is the drop (bindu), the cause of both origination and persistence.
Just as butter arises from milk within the mind, so too does the drop arise; though it exists within the midst of bondage, that indeed is the mental cause.
The power (śakti) that resides between the moon and the sun is bondage;
having understood this, one should pierce the suṣumnā and cause the vital breath (vāyu) to enter the middle path.
Having stationed himself in the location of the Bindu, he should restrain the breath within the nostrils—
the breath being called the Bindu, as well as Sattva and Prakṛti.
Having fully understood the six wheels, one should enter the mandala of bliss:
the mūlādhāra, the svādhiṣṭhāna, and the maṇipūra as the third.
The unstruck (anāhata), the pure (viśuddhi), and the wheel of command (ājñācakra) as the sixth;
the support (ādhāra) is said to be the anus, while the self-consecrated (svādhiṣṭhāna) is located in the genitals. || 10 ||
Maṇipūra is in the region of the navel; Anāhata is situated in the heart; Viśuddhi is at the root of the throat; and the Ājñā-cakra is at the head. (11)

"One should characterize [the self] as 'I am Brahman' through the vision of the full moon (*pūrṇimādṛṣṭi*), preceded by the abandonment of the conceptualization of objects and their subjects"—thus he says: "By desire" (*kāmena*). Furthermore: "In the midst of power" (*śaktimadhye*).
Having fixed the mind, characterized by the vision of the full moon, in the midst of the *kuṇḍalinī* power, once again...
Having also placed the mind within the power [of the breath],

with a mind transformed into the form of Brahman, one should perceive "I am Brahman"— the substratum for the negation of the mind and its effects— and then abandon even that mental modification consisting of such perception; for that alone is [the goal].

The "supreme state" means absolute liberation (*kaivalya*). (4) To the question "What is that mind? he says: "Mind. Because the mind is the cause of the emergence and so forth of the individual phenomenal world (*vyaṣṭi-prapañca*), it is itself the *bindu*, the Lord (*īśvara*);
for there is a scriptural text stating, "The *bindu* is known by the name of the Lord. (5) Or else: the *bindu* is produced from the mind.
Because the conceptualization of the *bindu* and so forth has the mind as its cause, it is an effect of the mind;

this is according to the statement of the venerable teacher Bhagavatpāda: "The Lord was conceptualized by me. Just as milk is of the nature of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), so too the *bindu* is of the nature of the mind—this is the meaning. Regarding the point that the principle of the Lord (*īśvaratattva*) is bound by the mind, he says: [the following verse].

It is situated within bondage because of the unreality of the mind. Nor does that [bondage] become identical with its own cause, the mind, as in the case of the individual mind; for when the mind has ceased, the Bindu—the Lord—is nothing but the undifferentiated Brahman. (6) He states that bondage is indeed distinct from the Lord:

Regarding the word "candre" (in the moon): having understood that the mind is bound where the Śakti Kuṇḍalinī resides— situated between the moon and the sun at the seat of the *brahmarandhra* and *mūlādhāra*—
and having realized that the binding of the mind is the activity of the Kuṇḍalinī which is distinct from oneself, one strives for its uprooting.

There are three knots in the *suṣumnā*; having pierced them and having caused the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the other winds to enter the center of that *suṣumnā*, one should remain at the station of *bindu*— the space between the eyebrows and so forth— thinking "I am the Lord named *bindu*," and having steadied the wind, one should restrain it within the aperture of the vital breath.
The meaning is that one should perform only the *kevalakumbhaka* (pure retention). Having understood the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, one should enter into the bliss of yoga;
thus he says: "the wind" (verse 8). To the question of what the six wheels (*cakras*) are, he says: "the root" (verse 9).
Through the practice of breath, one attains the form of Virāj; having fully understood the six wheels, one should enter the sphere of bliss.
Having drawn in the wind, one should enter it and direct it upward by that very [channel]. || 12 ||
One who practices the breath in this manner shall become identical with the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa).
One should likewise practice the breath, the bindu, the cakras, and the mind.
Thus, the meaning is that through the practice of *prāṇa*, one becomes of the nature of Virāj.
The meaning is that, having unified the mind and the *prāṇa*, one should practice yoga preceded by meditation on the *bindu* within the six *cakras*. || 12-13 ||
Without the yoga of practice, there is no manifestation of one's own Self;
through samādhi alone, yogis attain the equal nectar. Just as fire dwelling within wood does not rise up without friction, [so it is with the Self]. (14)
Indeed, without the practice of yoga, the lamp of knowledge does not shine forth;
just as a lamp placed inside a jar does not illuminate the outside. (15)
When that jar has been broken, the flame of the lamp still shines;
one's own body is called the "jar," and the lamp is indeed that [ultimate] state. (16)

Through a single non-conceptual yoga, yogis attain the immortal Brahman, which is equanimity and total equality. Thus, he states with an illustration that without the yoga of practice, one's own Self does not manifest:
"Just as... (verses 14–15). One's own body stands in the place of the jar.
Thus he was addressed. || 16 ||
Through the instruction of the Guru, the knowledge of Brahman arises;

when that knowledge of Brahman becomes one with the words of the Guru, it becomes manifest. Having obtained the Guru as their helmsman and having made [the mind] subtle, they cross over [the ocean of saṃsāra]. (17)

By the power of the latent impressions of practice, they cross the ocean of worldly existence. Once the veil of one's own ignorance has been pierced by the words of the Guru, there arises the knowledge of Brahman; having approached the Guru and made the meaning taught by him into a boat. (17)
Brahman, which is the substratum of the activity of speech, having become a sprout in the *parā* [state], is made into two petals in the *paśyantī* [state]. (18)

That speech which was previously described as being first in the *madhyamā* state, [then] budding in the *paśyantī*, and fully blossomed in the *vaikharī*, becomes set at rest through the reverse process. (19)
The Supreme God, the immutable one who awakens speech, is the source of that speech;
the man who always abides having ascertained "I am He" [is liberated]. || 20 ||
Even when addressed with various high and low words, he is not defiled.
Regarding how those who perceive the phenomenal world of worldly convention cross the ocean of existence, it is said:
[the arising, maintenance, and dissolution of the functions of speech that sustain the phenomenal world of worldly convention].

He says that they go to the state of Brahman on the far shore of the ocean of existence with the words "to the Supreme" (*parāya*). Regarding the activity of speech: "Speech is measured in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them."
Three [quarters] of speech are hidden in the cave and do not stir; humans speak only the fourth.
Thus, in accordance with the Śruti, having sprouted within Parā located in the *mūlādhāra*,
[it develops] within Paśyantī located in the *anāhata* [cakra], within Madhyamā located in the *viśuddhi-cakra*,
and within Vaikharī located in the mouth. (18–20)
Brahman is the substratum of the manifold universe beginning with Viśva;
and those three are Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña. || 21 ||
Virāṭ, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Īśvara—these are the three;
as well as the macrocosm (brahmāṇḍa), the microcosm (piṇḍāṇḍa), and the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, in their respective order.
(334) They dissolve into the inner self (pratyagātman) precisely through the dissolution of their respective limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
The cosmic egg (aṇḍa), heated by the fire of knowledge, dissolves along with its causal principles (kāraṇa). || 23 ||
When that [individual self] is merged into the Supreme Self, it becomes none other than the Supreme Brahman itself.

Raising the objection—given the distinctions such as Viśva and Virāṭ, which depend upon the individual (vyaṣṭi) and collective (samaṣṭi) manifestations of the phenomenal world—how can the knower remain as the Supreme Brahman on the far shore of the ocean of worldly existence? To this, if you [should say]:

When there is the delusion that the common phenomenal world exists as something separate from oneself, then through the knowledge of one's own true nature, the phenomenal world of one's own ignorance dissolves;
and by means of the knowledge of Brahman alone— the impossibility of anything other than oneself— that substratum of dissolution becomes substrate-less.
He says, "And the universe," [meaning] that only one's own non-dual self remains. (21–23)

The meaning is that what is imagined as something separate from oneself by the vision of one's own ignorance, having dissolved through the vision of one's own knowledge, becomes Brahman alone from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Brahman is beyond all comparison;
therefore, it is still and profound, neither light nor pervasive darkness.
Something remains that is unnameable and unmanifest; yet, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭi*), how does that become Brahman? To this he says: "From that" (*tataḥ*).

Since, from the perspective of one's own ignorance and so forth, there arises the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as something separate from oneself, and even its subsequent negation (*apavāda*), therefore—

From the vision of the reality of things, it is as motionless and profound as the quality-less, partless ether; because there is no possibility of delimitation by the elements, their derivatives, light, or darkness, it is neither light nor pervading darkness. // 24 //

Likewise, due to the non-occurrence of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), there remains nothing whatsoever—whether the delusion of one's own ignorance and so forth exists or does not exist—that is unnameable and unmanifest; for the Śruti declares, "Brahman alone is, not the non-existent."
Having meditated upon the self situated within, like a lamp inside a jar, as the meditation that serves as the means for attaining Brahman; || 25 ||
One should meditate upon the self, the size of a thumb, which is smokeless and of the nature of light, abiding within, immutable, and imperishable.
Likewise, the conscious self within the body, deluded by *māyā* through the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, subsequently undergoes many further births. (27)
But through the ripening of past good deeds, it desires to effect its own transformation, thinking:
"Who am I? How has this defect called 'saṃsāra' come upon me? (28)
"Where is my course when I am active in the waking state, dreaming, or in deep sleep?"—becoming intent on such reflection, and especially through his own inner radiance, [he realized this]. (29)
But when the appearance of consciousness is heated by external heat due to ignorance, it is indeed consumed, like a bundle of cotton by fire. (30)
The inner self, residing within the heart, once knowledge has perished, thereafter expands and,
having pervaded all, consumes even that consciousness in an instant.
Having thoroughly burned away those consisting of mind and those consisting of knowledge,
it shines eternally within itself alone, like a lamp inside a jar.
Thus, he states the means for the realization of Brahman alone, which is devoid of all counterparts: "Having meditated," and so forth.
25-26 || By its own nature, the conscious self—even though it is the Supreme Self—wanders in saṃsāra due to the conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding that which is other than itself;
however, by virtue of the ripening of the good deeds accumulated over many millions of births, it becomes oriented toward the innermost Self (pratyagātman); thereafter—
He says that [the Self] remains as the nature of the disembodied liberated self (videhamukta), which is free from the temporal flux of the manifold world imagined by one's own ignorance—thus:
"The conscious self" (vijñānātman). (27–33)
The sage who remains thus absorbed in meditation from birth until death, attaining both liberation while living and liberation after the body has fallen away—
he is to be known as one liberated while living; he is blessed and has accomplished his purpose.

Having abandoned the state of one liberated while living when his own body has been surrendered to time, he enters the state of disembodied liberation, just as the wind enters a state of motionlessness. (34)
That which is soundless, touchless, formless, imperishable, likewise tasteless, eternal, and odorless;
that which is without beginning or end, greater than the great, fixed—that alone remains, stainless and free from affliction.
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.

When the identification with the body, which has taken deep root in one's own person, is surrendered to Time and undergoes a transformation into a distorted dissolution, then, simultaneously with the awakening that brings about the cessation of the conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth, only one's own true nature remains— this is the meaning. (34) [This occurs] while the phenomenal world of sound and the rest still exists for one who is liberated while in the body (videhamukta).
To the question "How is it merely one's own Self?", he says: "It is wordless" (*aśabdam*).

There is no dispute regarding the fact that Brahman—the nature of disembodied liberation established through the negation of everything—is one's own non-dual Self alone. This is so even from the perspective of those lacking self-knowledge (*svājña*).

When there is the modification of sound and so forth, then from the perspective of one who knows itself, that which is the substratum for the dissolution of sound and so forth becomes distinguished by the absence of specific qualities such as sound; that very same [reality], from the perspective of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-dṛṣṭi), remains as its own non-dual, peerless nature alone—this is the meaning. || 35 ||
The word "iti" followed by "upaniṣat" signifies the conclusion of the Yogakuṇḍalī Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the third chapter. The commentary on the Yogakuṇḍalī Upaniṣad has been clearly written by Upadeśabrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra.
The commentary on the Kuṇḍalī Upaniṣad is recorded as consisting of two hundred [verses].

Thus ends the commentary on the Yogakuṇḍalī Upaniṣad, completing the eighty-sixth [treatise] in the venerable exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Īśā.
